edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 1, Paris 1844), De baptismo, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Hic ergo scelestissimi illi provocant quaestiones. Adeo, dicunt, Baptismus non est necessarius, quibus fides satis est, nam et Abraham nullius aquae nisi fidei sacramento Deo placuit. Sed in omnibus posteriora concludunt, et sequentia antecedentibus praevalent. Fuerit salus retro per fidem nudam ante Domini passionem et resurrectionem. At ubi fides aucta est credendi in nativitatem, passionem, resurrectionemque ejus, addita est ampliatio sacramento, obsignatio Baptismi vestimentum quodammodo fidei, quae retro erat nuda, nec potentiam habuit sine sua lege. Lex enim tinguendi imposita est, et forma praescripta. Ite, inquit, docete nationes, tinguentes eas in nomine Patris et Filii et Spiritus sancti. Huic legi collata definitio illa: Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua et spiritu, non intrabit in regnum coelorum, obstrinxit fidem ad Baptismi necessitatem. Itaque omnes exinde credentes tinguebantur. Tunc et Paulus ubi credidit, tinctus est. Et hoc est quod Dominus in illa plaga orbationis praeceperat: Exsurge, dicens, et introi Damascum, illic tibi demonstrabitur quid debeas agere, scilicet tingui, quod solum ei deerat. Alioquin satis didicerat atque crediderat Nazarenum esse Dominum Dei Filium.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, those most wicked ones provoke these questions. So, they say, Baptism is not necessary for those for whom faith is enough, for even Abraham pleased God by the sacrament of faith without any water. But in all things, later things conclude and following things prevail over preceding ones. Salvation was able to be in the past through bare faith before the Lord's passion and resurrection. But when faith was increased by believing in His birth, passion, and resurrection, an amplification of the sacrament was added, a sealing of Baptism, a kind of garment of faith, which was previously bare and did not have power without its own law. For the law of baptizing was imposed and a form was prescribed. Go, He says, teach the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. To this law, that definition was added: Unless someone is born again from water and spirit, he will not enter into the kingdom of heaven, which bound faith to the necessity of Baptism. And so, from then on, all believers were baptized. Then also Paul, when he believed, was baptized. And this is what the Lord commanded in that stroke of blindness: Arise, He says, and enter into Damascus, there it will be shown to you what you ought to do, namely to be baptized, which alone was lacking to him. Otherwise, he had learned enough and had believed that the Nazarene is the Lord, the Son of God.

bible_refs.note: Go, teach the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit
Unless someone is born again from water and spirit, he will not enter into the kingdom of heaven

pass_b_english: Those most wicked characters raise these questions. They claim baptism isn't necessary for people who have faith, since Abraham pleased God through the sacrament of faith without any water at all. But in everything, the later revelation settles the matter, and what comes after overrides what came before. Salvation used to be possible through bare faith before the Lord's passion and resurrection. Once faith expanded to include belief in his birth, passion, and resurrection, the sacrament was amplified—baptism was added as a seal, a kind of garment for faith that had previously stood naked and lacked power without its own law. The law of baptism was imposed, and a form was prescribed: "Go, make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matt 28:19). To that law was appended the definition: "Unless someone is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God" (John 3:5), which bound faith to the necessity of baptism. From then on, all who believed were baptized. Even Paul, the moment he believed, was baptized. This is exactly what the Lord commanded in that stroke of blindness: "Get up and go into Damascus; there you will be told what you must do" (Acts 22:10)—namely, be baptized, the one thing he still lacked. He had already learned and believed thoroughly that the Nazarene is the Lord, the Son of God.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, and Pass B provides a fluent English version that correctly identifies and cites the embedded scriptural allusions (Matt 28:19, John 3:5, Acts 22:10) which were present in the Latin but required identification as per the instructions. All clauses, including the nuances of 'fides nuda' and the causal relationship between the new law and the necessity of baptism, are preserved.
